name: Whakaari/White Island
title: Whakaari/White Island Volcano: Alert Level & 2019 Eruption
description: Whakaari/White Island, New Zealand’s most active volcano: GeoNet’s Level 2 in November 2026, the October eruption, the 2019 disaster and its record.
since_check: **Volcanic Alert Level 2, on New Zealand’s scale of 0 to 5.** GeoNet lowered the level from 3 to 2 and the aviation color code to yellow on November 2, 2026: since Thursday, October 29, no observations had pointed to eruptive activity.[[geonet]][[geonetvab]] Level 2 stands for moderate to heightened unrest, with the potential for eruption hazards.[[geonetval]]
lede: Whakaari/White Island is an uninhabited volcanic island in New Zealand’s Bay of Plenty and the country’s most active volcano. It erupted weakly in October 2026, and in December 2019 an explosion killed 22 of the 47 people on the island. Below: its state now, what New Zealand’s alert levels mean, the 2019 eruption, the deaths on record, the dangers, its height and every eruption on record.
answer: **Whakaari/White Island is not erupting.** GeoNet reported a weak eruption of ash in **October 2026** and lowered the alert level to **2** on November 2, after no sign of eruptive activity since October 29.[[geonet]][[geonetvab]] The Smithsonian’s list ends earlier, with the eruption of {last_span}.[[gvp]] The island’s highest point is **{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m)** above the sea.[[gnsfact]]

paras: Whakaari/White Island is a volcanic island in the Bay of Plenty of [New Zealand](/volcanoes-in-new-zealand), about 30 miles (48 km) offshore by GeoNet’s figure, north-east of Whakatāne.[[geonetabout]][[teara]] It is about 1.2 miles (2 km) across and covers about 800 acres (325 hectares), and no one lives on it.[[gnsfact]][[geonetabout]] The Smithsonian places the volcano at {coords}.[[gvp]]

Its Māori name, Te Puia o Whakaari, means to make visible, GNS Science writes.[[gnsfact]] The island is important to the Ngāti Awa and Te Whakatōhea tribes, and it is a privately owned scenic reserve.[[teara]][[gnsfact]]
Whakaari is one of {n_country} volcanoes in New Zealand on the Smithsonian’s Holocene list; [Ruapehu](/volcano/ruapehu) and [Taranaki](/volcano/taranaki) are two others.[[gvp]]

No. GeoNet, which watches New Zealand’s volcanoes, lowered the alert level to 2 on November 2, 2026, because since Thursday, October 29, no observations had pointed to eruptive activity.[[geonet]][[geonetvab]]

The eruption itself was weak. On October 19 GeoNet reported low, intermittent plumes of steam and gas with minor ash. On October 21 it raised the level to 3 and the aviation color code to orange, writing that the volcano was now continuously, passively erupting a small amount of ash, and on October 27 low plumes of ash and gas were still rising.[[geonet]]
The Smithsonian’s list ends earlier, with the eruption of {last_span}.[[gvp]]

sections.h: What does Alert Level 2 mean at Whakaari?
paras: New Zealand’s volcanic alert levels run from 0 to 5. Levels 1 and 2 mean unrest; Levels 3, 4 and 5 mean an eruption is under way, from minor to major.[[geonetval]]

Level 2 is moderate to heightened unrest, with unrest hazards and the potential for eruption hazards. Level 3, in force from October 21 to November 2, 2026, means a minor eruption, with hazards near the vent.[[geonetval]][[geonet]]
An eruption may occur at any level, and the levels need not move in order, GeoNet warns. Earth Sciences New Zealand sets the level from the volcano’s activity.[[geonetval]]

At 2:11 p.m. Whakaari erupted while 47 people were on the island: tourists, 38 of them passengers of the cruise ship Ovation of the Seas, and their guides.[[nzhist2019]] Steam and volcanic gas burst out without warning, and the blast threw rock high into the air; NOAA’s record describes an ash plume and a pyroclastic surge across the whole crater area.[[nzhist2019]][[noaa]] The blast came from vents in the 1978/90 Crater Complex, and it emptied the crater lake, opened new vents and set off landslides into the active crater, GeoNet writes.[[geonetabout]]
Twenty-two people died, at once or later, of burns or respiratory injuries, and 25 were injured, most of them critically. The bodies of two were never recovered.[[coroners]][[nzhist2019]]

The crew and passengers of a nearby boat rescued 23 people straight away, and three commercial helicopter pilots landed on the island while it was still erupting and rescued 12 more.[[nzhist2019]] A coroner’s inquiry into the deaths began its second phase in Auckland on September 14, 2026.[[coroners]]

sections.h: How many people has Whakaari killed?
paras: NOAA’s database of significant eruptions has {noaa_n_word} entries for Whakaari, {noaa_first} and {noaa_last}, with {noaa_deaths} deaths between them.[[noaa]]

The first was not an eruption. On September 10, 1914, part of the crater wall collapsed, and the landslide overwhelmed the camp of the men working the island’s sulfur. NOAA’s note and GNS Science count 11 sulfur miners killed; New Zealand’s Ministry for Culture and Heritage counts 10.[[noaa]][[gnsfact]][[nzhist1914]]
The second is the eruption of {worst_date}, with {worst_deaths} deaths and {worst_injuries} people injured.[[noaa]]

sections.note: This page is a record, not a safety guide. For the current alert level, follow GeoNet.
paras: Yes, above all in its crater. Whakaari can erupt suddenly: in 2019 an explosion of steam and gas struck while 47 people were on the island.[[nzhist2019]]

During the eruption of October 2026, GeoNet warned that sudden, more explosive eruptions could threaten anyone on the crater floor and on the sea to the south-east.[[geonet]] New Zealand’s scale adds that an eruption may come at any alert level.[[geonetval]]
Until the 2019 eruption, up to 10,000 tourists a year came by boat or helicopter, Te Ara writes.[[teara]]

Before them came the sulfur miners. Sulfur was mined at intervals from the 1880s to the 1930s, and the remains of a factory are still on the island, GNS Science writes.[[gnsfact]] In 1914 a landslide overwhelmed the workers’ camp.[[teara]]

Earth Sciences New Zealand, through GeoNet, which sets the alert level.[[geonetval]] It no longer has working monitoring equipment on the island: it watches the volcano from regular observation and gas flights, from webcams on the mainland at Te Kaha and Whakatāne, and by satellite and other remote methods.[[geonetmon]]
**{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m)** above sea level at its highest point, GNS Science says; the Smithsonian’s list gives {gvp_summit_m} m.[[gnsfact]][[gvp]]
The crater floor lies less than 100 ft (30 m) above the sea, and about 70 percent of the volcano is under water.[[gnsfact]]

sections.h: What type of volcano is Whakaari?
paras: A stratovolcano, made of {rock}, by the Smithsonian.[[gvp]] GeoNet calls it New Zealand’s most active cone volcano, built up by continuous activity over the past 150,000 years.[[geonetabout]]
The Smithsonian counts {n_all} confirmed eruptions since {since_year}, every one of them known from written reports.[[gvp]]

Since {counted_year} it has erupted in long spells and short bursts; the longest on the list ran from {long1_span}, more than {long1_years} years.[[gvp]] GeoNet counts the years from December 1975 to September 2000 as one eruption episode, the longest and largest in the island’s recorded history.[[geonetabout]] GeoNet’s eruption of {agency_last} came {agency_gap} after the last one on the list ended.[[geonet]][[gvp]]
The Smithsonian’s record for Whakaari/White Island has **{n_all} confirmed eruptions**, all of them known from written reports.[[gvp]]

faq: No. GeoNet lowered its alert level to 2 on November 2, 2026, after no sign of eruptive activity since October 29. It had confirmed a weak eruption of ash on October 21.
Level 2, moderate to heightened unrest, on New Zealand’s scale of 0 to 5, since November 2, 2026. It was at Level 3, a minor eruption, from October 21.
In October 2026: a weak, continuous release of ash that GeoNet confirmed on October 21 and that had stopped by October 29. The last eruption on the Smithsonian’s list ran from {last_span}.
At 2:11 p.m. on December 9, 2019, a sudden explosion of steam and gas struck while 47 people were on the island. Twenty-two died and 25 were injured, most of them critically.
How far is Whakaari from the mainland?
About 30 miles (48 km) offshore in the Bay of Plenty, north-east of Whakatāne, by GeoNet’s figure.
{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m) above sea level at its highest point, by GNS Science’s figure. About 70 percent of the volcano is under the sea.
It is privately owned and is a scenic reserve, Te Ara writes. The island is important to the Ngāti Awa and Te Whakatōhea tribes.
